Series::pull¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

template<class T>
std::vector<T> Series::pull() const

Crossing A One-Dimensional Series Into C++¶

pull<T>() materializes a rank-one Series as an owning std::vector<T>. It is the direct companion to item<T>(): item() crosses the host boundary for shape [], while pull() crosses it for shape [n].

The rank check is intentional. A matrix is not silently flattened, and a scalar is not silently wrapped in a one-element vector. Generic code that must accept arbitrary rank should use host<T>(), where shape and stride metadata remain available.

T selects the C++ element representation. The Series is converted while it is materialized, so a floating Series may be pulled as double, an integer Series as std::int64_t, and a Boolean Series as bool. Conversion follows the same dtype rules as Series::to(...).

Ownership, Placement, And Cost¶

The returned vector owns its allocation. Changing it cannot mutate the Series, and later Series mutations cannot change the vector. A non-CPU receiver is synchronized and copied to host memory before conversion. Consequently, pull() belongs at an interoperability, logging, serialization, or testing boundary—not inside a per-lane numerical loop.

pull() is not differentiable because std::vector<T> has no Series graph identity. The receiver and its graph are unchanged; only the extracted C++ copy lies outside reverse mode.

Examples¶

1. Pull a floating vector¶

const auto values = pluss::make_series({1.25, 2.5, 5.0});
const auto host = values.pull<double>();

for (double value : host) std::cout << value << ' ';
std::cout << '\n';

Output¶

1.25 2.5 5

The auto variable is an ordinary std::vector<double> because pull() has one fixed native return type.

2. Convert the element representation while pulling¶

const auto values = pluss::make_series({2, 4, 8});
const std::vector<double> host = values.pull<double>();

std::cout << host.size() << ' ' << host.front() << ' ' << host.back() << '\n';

Output¶

3 2 8

The Series remains integral. Only the owning host copy uses double.

3. Preserve an empty one-dimensional shape¶

const auto empty = pluss::series::empty({0}, pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
const auto host = empty.pull<double>();

std::cout << "dim=" << empty.dim()
          << " size=" << host.size() << '\n';

Output¶

dim=1 size=0

An empty vector is still rank one, so it satisfies the contract.

4. Pull a Boolean mask¶

const auto mask = pluss::make_series({true, false, true});
const auto host = mask.pull<bool>();

std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << host[0] << ' ' << host[1] << ' ' << host[2] << '\n';

Output¶

true false true

The result is std::vector<bool>, including its standard packed Boolean storage behavior.

5. Reject scalar and matrix receivers¶

for (const auto& value : {
         pluss::make_series(7),
         pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3, 4}, {2, 2})}) {
  try {
    (void)value.pull<std::int64_t>();
  } catch (const std::exception& error) {
    std::cout << error.what() << '\n';
  }
}

Output¶

Series::pull<T>(): expected a rank-one Series
Series::pull<T>(): expected a rank-one Series

Use item<T>() for the scalar. Use host<T>() for the matrix instead of discarding its two-dimensional structure.
